problem: End-to-end Seq2Seq/transformer agents on ALFRED map long instructions directly to trivial actions, overfit to training-scene visuals (large seen-to-unseen drop), and give humans no way to check whether the instruction was understood correctly before the agent acts.
motivation: Human-agent interaction (e.g. household robots) needs interpretability and the ability to monitor an agent's plan before execution. Humans first form an expectation of sub-steps and then act; decoupling language understanding from action execution should also reduce overfitting to scene visuals.
key_idea: Split the agent into two streams: a BART-based language expectation module that turns step-by-step instructions plus scene-object prior into an inspectable sub-step and object sequence, and a binding policy that executes each sub-step with map-based FMM navigation and fixed atomic-action manipulation scripts.
insight: Separating planning (language) from execution (map, segmentation, scripted actions) keeps unseen performance close to seen performance (valid SR 27.63 seen vs 22.36 unseen), whereas end-to-end methods such as ABP, LWIT and EmBERT drop sharply. The ground-truth ablation shows that perception, especially segmentation, is the bottleneck: +gt seg gives +18.0/+11.8 SR on seen/unseen, versus only +1.8/+1.7 for +gt depth.
method: Language Expectation: BART on concatenated step-by-step instruction tokens plus scene object embedding O_p (from exploration); two BART heads output a sub-step sequence A and an object sequence O, which humans can inspect before execution
Map construction: predicted depth and semantic segmentation from RGB give a semantic point cloud, projected to a 0/1 obstacle map V_t (0.25 m grid) using height thresholds against agent height
Object memory: DBSCAN clusters the points of each observed object category and the cluster center is stored as the object location
Scene exploration: before the task, the agent samples unexplored coordinates until all are seen, so the map and object memory are near-complete
FMM navigation: Fast Marching Method plans a path from agent position to the target object's location on the map, replanned at every step as the map updates
Determined manipulation policy: each manipulation type (e.g. Heat) maps to a fixed sequence of atomic actions (Open, Close, PickUp, Put, ToggleOn, ToggleOff), using the object's pixel mask

setting.backbone: BART (fine-tuned) for language expectation + learned depth and semantic segmentation models (frozen after training); FMM and scripted manipulation are non-learned
setting.training_data: ALFRED training set only (21,023 tasks; expert demonstrations and step-by-step instructions); no extra language or visual-augmentation data
setting.observation: egocentric RGB only (depth and segmentation are predicted from RGB)
setting.action_space: low-level ALFRED actions (Move/Turn navigation via FMM waypoints, plus Pick/Put/Open/Close/Toggle manipulation scripts)
setting.privileged: none for the main results (an initial exploration of the scene is done before each task); GT depth/segmentation only in the ablation

numbers.extra: step-by-step instructions only (no goal description); initial scene exploration
test-seen leaderboard split; step-by-step instructions only

numbers.backbone: BART + GT depth and GT segmentation

numbers_note: ALFRED is not in the canonical benchmark list, so the bench name 'ALFRED' is used. Metrics are SR and GC (goal-condition success); PLW metrics are not reported.
results: LEBP reaches 24.26 SR / 30.49 GC on test-unseen and 22.36 SR on valid-unseen using only step-by-step instructions. That beats the best goal-description-only method HLSM (20.27 test-unseen SR, 18.28 valid-unseen SR) and beats FILM on valid-unseen SR (20.10), although FILM (26.49) is higher on test-unseen SR. The seen-to-unseen gap is small.
limitations: Perception is the bottleneck: segmentation errors limit performance, and GC is much higher than SR on Clean/Cool/Heat tasks, meaning one failed sub-task fails the whole task
Requires an initial full-scene exploration before each task, which is costly and assumes a static scene
Scripted manipulation and text-only expectation are fixed; the interactive human check is proposed but never evaluated
